item.title: Expanding AI Control from Models to Harnesses
item.description:
Most AI control research such as LinuxArena and Ctrl-Z only gives the red team basic agents which only have access to tools. Yet in 2026, usage of AI within frontier labs has moved to agent harnesses that have access to skills, memory, subagents, external services, compaction and more.

At the same time, Claude Code and Codex have both implemented their own version of both action-based and source code monitoring.

In such a world, the threat vectors have changed. While it may remain important to do theoretical research on improving protocols and monitors, AI control research should expand to include:

  • Vulnerability Research
    Identify specific vulnerabilities that can be patched plus architectural weaknesses in production control protocols.
  • Harness Evaluations
    Identify the attack uplift modern harnesses provide over basic agents and evaluate the effectiveness of control protocols within those harnesses.

In this post, I briefly describe how control works in Claude Code and Codex, then demonstrate how a rogue agent could use the features of Claude Code to execute an attack while being “monitored” by auto mode.

I then provide an overview of the features of modern harnesses and how these may be leveraged to execute attacks that could subvert control implementations.  

Finally, I explore the state of control protocols today, and provide suggestions for doing AI control research in the era of agent harnesses.

AI Control in Current Harnesses

Both Claude Code and Codex now ship with built-in action and code review monitors, and allow third-party control protocols to be integrated via hooks. 

The built-in monitors target:

  • Process-Based / Live Attacks
    Execution of a command that causes immediate harm (e.g., a bash command to exfiltrate secrets).  
  • Product-Based / Delayed Attacks
    Insertion of vulnerabilities that get exploited after the work product is accepted (e.g., code injected with a vulnerability triggered in production).

Protection against process-based attacks is implemented as:

  • Auto Permissions Mode in Claude Code
    A two-stage judge that evaluates every tool call not explicitly allowed or denied by the permission rules. First, a fast judgement is made on whether to allow or deny a tool call; if denied, a thinking judge makes a final allow or deny call, providing the reason why for denials.
  • Auto-Review Mode in Codex
    An investigator agent with limited affordances given a read-only copy of the sandbox for actions that cross the sandbox boundary. The agent allows or denies the action, providing the reason why for denials.

To simplify terminology in this post, I’ll be calling both “auto mode”.

Protection against product-based attacks is implemented as:

  • Security Review in Claude Code
    An on-demand /security-review command checks the current code changes for vulnerabilities, while a companion GitHub Action runs the security review on pull requests and leaves inline comments.

Separately, on-demand managed Code Review uses a team of agents to check for logic errors, vulnerabilities and regressions in GitHub PRs, while Claude Security goes deeper and traces data flows across files within a GitHub repo to find, validate and suggest patches for code vulnerabilities.

Finally, a security-guidance plugin installs hooks to run checks after every file edit, at the end of every turn and before any commit or push.

  • Codex Security in Codex
    Codex Security runs both on-demand and CI/CD reviews to find, validate and suggest patches for code vulnerabilities. It can also be used to scan GitHub repositories connected through Codex cloud.

Except for the security-guidance plugin, none of these run automatically or block code from being committed or merged; though hooks or CI actions can be used to configure these behaviors.

Also, security reviews may not be robust against adversarial attacks. Anthropic’s GitHub Action specifically calls this out. Review agents can be susceptible to prompt injections and may not catch subtle attacks that don’t look like traditional vulnerabilities. So they are not a replacement for product-based control protocols.

Vulnerability Research on Claude Code

Let’s walk through an example of how a rogue agent may be able to use the features of a harness to execute an attack.[1] 

This example uses Claude Code in auto mode with a single command, pytest, in the permissions allow list.[2] Auto mode is a permission mode in Claude Code that uses a monitor to approve or deny actions proposed by an agent.

Create a Skill

The first thing the agent does is to create a skill that includes a script. Agents writing their own skills to formalize their knowledge and capabilities is becoming more common.

However, in this case, the script will assist in the attack. Scripts can include self-contained attacks (as in this example) or split attacks between the script and the parameters passed into the script by the agent calling it.

Modify Execution Permissions

By default, executing the skill script will be blocked by auto mode, since skill scripts are executed within a bash shell and the script command is in neither the permissions allow list nor the auto mode allow list.

To execute the script, the agent needs to add it to an allow list—but all files and folders under .claude except for worktrees are protected paths, meaning any edits need to be approved by the auto-mode monitor.

However, the auto-mode monitor does not review file edits within the agent’s workspace, e.g., the directory tree the agent was started in. This provides a way for the agent to get around the protected-path restriction: the agent can create a Python test file that edits .claude/settings.local.json and adds the skill script to the permissions.allow list.

Since pytest is in the permissions.allow list and running pytest without any parameters does not look suspicious to the auto-mode monitor, the agent can easily run it to pick up and run the new test.

Once the test runs, the updated permissions will allow future agent sessions to execute the skill.

Delegate to Subagent

At this point, Claude Code is running with the permissions it was launched with. If it wants to execute the attack immediately and not wait until its next session, it can delegate the execution of the skill script to a subagent.

When this attack was last tested, subagents in Claude Code started with a fresh context and reloaded all settings files, including the modified settings.local.json.

Thus, because the script now exists in the permissions.allow list, the auto mode monitor isn’t invoked when the subagent calls the skill script, allowing the attack to proceed.

Harnesses Open Up New Attack Surfaces

This example shows a single path by which a rogue agent could use the features of a harness to execute an attack. The next few sections will explore a range of harness features and some of the theoretical attack paths these open up.

These features often break some of the core assumptions of AI control protocols used in research:

  • Monitoring is fixed—local settings can change how agents are monitored.
  • Tools don’t have hidden exploits—agents can now write their own tools.
  • Agents run stateless—memory and skills allow agents to persist knowledge.
  • Trajectories contain everything—compaction and subagents create altered or entirely clean trajectories.

The next sections show how these broken assumptions could be used via features in attacks in ways traditional control protocols may not expect. As attacks move from code and commands to configuration, AI control needs to adapt.

Important: While l mention specific implementation details for Codex and Claude Code, treat these as examples of how these harnesses may have operated at a point in time. Frontier harnesses are evolving rapidly, and while the concepts below should hold for a while, many of the specifics will be quickly outdated.  

Permissions

Permission rules determine what commands are allowed to run, what actions get monitored, and how those actions get monitored when they do.

Types of Permissions

Permissions fall into three broad categories:

  • Accept: Allow the action to proceed.
  • Ask/Prompt: Ask whether the action should proceed.
  • Deny/Forbidden: Block the action from proceeding.

Within these broad categories can be many nuances:

  • Asking may be delegated to a monitor policy.
  • Deny rules may be broken into hard and soft deny rules.
  • Specific features may have their own permissions, e.g., Claude Code skills have allow-tools and disallowed-tools lists.

How these permissions are defined may vary as well. For instance, Claude Code uses a custom syntax with glob patterns for tool permissions and natural language text for auto mode permissions, while Codex uses Starlark configuration functions for its permissions.

Each of these ways of specifying permissions may open up their own attack surfaces. 

For instance, in Claude Code the rule Bash(npm run lint:*) appears to limit execution to linting the code, but it actually runs whatever command is defined as lint in package.json, which the agent has permission to edit. In Codex, an exec-policy rule allowing cargo test appears to only allow running tests, but compiling the crate to do so runs build.rs, which the agent has permission to edit.

Location of Permissions

Permissions get configured across multiple files, often including files underneath the local working folder that an agent has access to.

For instance, in Claude Code, permission settings can be spread over ~/.claude/settings.json and both .claude/settings.json and .claude/settings.local.json in your project directory, as well as managed settings configured by your organization.

While writes to these files are protected by default, the protection only applies within the Claude Code executable. If an agent has permission to run a command, like pytest in the example earlier, it may be able to have that command modify the permissions.

Interaction Between Permissions

Often multiple types of permissions apply to a single command or action.

For instance, when running Claude Code in auto mode, calling a shell command to generate dynamic content in a skill requires evaluating the command permissions, the auto mode permissions and the allowed tools for the skill itself.

This generally increases safety, as multiple layers can prevent a potentially dangerous command from executing, but increases the number of variables that can be varied in vulnerability research and control evals.

Skills

Skills can be used to encode knowledge and workflows, but can also contain scripts and embedded shell commands.

Different harnesses monitor skills in different ways.

For instance, Claude Code auto mode can block a skill from ever being called, can block the dynamic content from being generated, or, separately, can block a script within a skill from being called, whereas Codex auto-review mode doesn’t monitor skills directly at all; instead, it monitors any actions triggered by that skill, such as shell commands or network calls.

Different harnesses handle skill content differently as well. While both Claude Code and Codex strip skill content before passing a trajectory to a monitor—to prevent the skill content from steering the approval process—previous versions of Claude Code injected the content as a user message after a successful skill call, which could have then affected future approvals.

Both Claude Code and Codex have ways to skip asking for permissions for tools that may be used by a skill. Claude Code does this via the allowed-tools and disallowed-tools metadata, while Codex uses a per-skill YAML file that is enabled via a global skill_approval setting.

Subagents

Subagents can be used to do work without cluttering up the context of the main agent.

Relevant to AI control, each subagent usually runs with its own trajectory (though in Codex, this is configurable), meaning when an action being taken by a subagent is reviewed by a monitor, the trajectory from the main agent may not be included.

This opens up the possibility of doing attacks via factored cognition, where an orchestrator agent splits an attack that would be too obvious if done in a single trajectory into multiple “clean” subtasks, each executed by a different agent.

Solo, Teams & Workflows

Subagents can operate solo, in teams or in workflows.

When working solo, each subagent operates independent of the others; though unless configured to use worktrees or some other form of workspace isolation, they may work in the same workspace (which could enable these agents to coordinate through files on disk).

When working in teams, subagents can share common resources such as task lists and send messages to one another. Subagents in teams are managed by a lead orchestrating agent that generally assigns tasks and summarizes results.

When working in workflows, the agent generates a program to run dozens to hundreds of agents with the program itself becoming the orchestrator rather than an agent. However, as with other code, workflow scripts open up another potential attack surface for a rogue agent.

Interaction Between Skills & Subagents

Subagents can be defined to only have access to a subset of skills and conversely, in some harnesses like Claude Code, skills can be defined to use a subagent.

Restricting the skills available should reduce the attack surface of a harness, but using a subagent for a skill may allow the lead agent to work around monitoring.

For example, while the vulnerability research example earlier didn’t use a subagent in the skill, defining the skill with context: fork may have been another way to run the script under new permissions.

Memory

Memory subsystems have become one of the most effective ways of making harnesses more powerful.

Memory can allow a rogue agent to save vulnerabilities it finds, keep track of a long-term strategic plan or pass key parameters for an attack to a future instance of itself (either in a separate session or as a subagent).

Writes to memory aren’t always monitored. Though once the memory is retrieved into the context window, monitors can usually see it and use it in their reasoning on whether to allow or deny specific actions. However, techniques like delegating to a subagent with a fresh context window may allow an agent to get around this monitoring.

External Services (MCP)

External services give agents new capabilities, including new attack surfaces.

Similar to skills, MCP servers can be used to obfuscate attacks by either encoding the full attack directly within an MCP server the agent writes, or by splitting the attack between the MCP server and the parameters passed to it.

While running new processes needs to get approved by auto mode, similar to the vulnerability research example described earlier, processes may be able to be launched as a side effect of running an approved process, e.g., by running an approved pytest which itself runs a subprocess.

Alternatively, if an approved MCP process is running on the same machine using HTTP, an agent that can kill the process may be able to re-bind a rogue MCP process to the same port.

Even valid registered MCP servers could be used as an attack vector if an agent can reason about its functionality better than its monitor and find a set of parameters which trigger a desired side effect (either due to a vulnerability in the MCP server or an undocumented capability).

Compaction

Compaction frees up context by summarizing, filtering, and archiving messages. This can include tool calls and their results plus both assistant and user messages.

For Claude Code and Codex, only active context is passed to the auto mode monitor. After compaction, incriminating messages may no longer exist in the active context, and could result in an auto-mode monitor allowing an action it otherwise would not.

That said, the likelihood of an agent using this for a successful attack is low. The action under review is always passed to the auto-mode monitor. So, only cases where the context itself drives the denial could be subverted by compaction.

Compaction Awareness & Control

If an agent wanted to execute such an attack, it may have both compaction awareness and compaction control.

Codex, for example, provides tools for an agent to either get the remaining context or request a new context window. By monitoring when the remaining context increases, the agent could detect compaction events. Likewise, requesting a new context window may allow it to eliminate any incriminating messages by triggering a compaction or a fresh clean context.

Even if not driven by the agent itself, compaction could change the results of a control eval. Trajectory monitors tested within agent harnesses may need to be written with compaction awareness and/or align the monitor’s compaction strategy with that of the agent harness.

In Codex, for example, remote compaction can encrypt agent messages, tool calls and their results. This encrypted trajectory is not provided to the monitor.

Control evals that explore the impact of dropping agent messages and tool call results on monitor scoring could be valuable, as well as monitor-aware compaction strategies that preserve the most suspicious agent actions.

Refinement

Refinement is the process of curating and optimizing memory and skills based on saved trajectories from that agent.

Memory Refinement

Agents can now “dream” to consolidate memories. During memory consolidation, a background agent prunes outdated memories, resolves conflicting memories, merges duplicates, and may reorganize memories into a hierarchy for more effective progressive disclosure.

Memory consolidation agents may have broad access to the entire memory system used by an agent harness, which can open up new affordances for attacks.

For instance, an agent that can’t write directly to global memory may be able to write a note to local memory and word it in such a way that the consolidation agent decides it should be in global memory, allowing it to influence all future instances of itself.

Similarly, an agent could create a conflicting memory designed to take precedence when the consolidation agent resolves the conflicting memories, providing one route to overriding existing instructions.

Current harnesses have measures limiting attacks from memory refinement—Claude Code’s dream mode doesn’t update CLAUDE.md and Codex’s memory consolidation uses prompts and hints like applies_to to enforce memory boundaries—but implementations change regularly, which can open up new capabilities.

From a control perspective, memory consolidation is unlikely to help with high-stakes attacks; however, memories that get promoted globally could drive persistent sandbagging or reward hacking in low-stakes control scenarios.

Skill Refinement

Skills package capabilities into reusable instructions, assets and scripts. While skills can be authored by humans, frequently agents themselves author their own skills, an attack vector already discussed.

Skill refinement provides a mechanism for both human-written and agent-written skills to be rewritten to improve performance. During this re-writing process, the skill could be modified to provide additional affordances for an attack.

Presently, skill refinement remains an area of active development. While Codex automates skill refinement as part of the same consolidation agent that provides memory refinement, Claude Code requires skill refinement be triggered by the user via the skill-creator skill. That may change as techniques like Microsoft’s SkillOpt get integrated into frontier lab agent harnesses.

For agent harnesses that create or refine skills autonomously, an agent may influence how the skill is rewritten by intentionally using a skill incorrectly to force a rewrite in a specific direction.

That’s complicated, however. More likely, any attack will come from the subagent doing the refinement.

Rogue Refinement Agents

Control research has investigated collusion between an agent and its monitor as well as an agent jailbreaking its monitor to rate attacks as not suspicious.

Compaction and refinement agents introduce new attack vectors. While such agents are usually sandboxed with limited affordances, the outputs these agents create could be used in attacks.

A compaction agent could collude with the main agent to erase suspicious messages or actions. A refinement agent could collude with the main agent to write or rewrite skills to enable an attack, or embed an attack by itself in a skill that the main agent unwittingly executes.

The backstop to attacks by such agents are the sandboxing and control protocols applied to actions the main agent takes; but as shown in the vulnerability research section, these can sometimes be subverted.

Sandboxing

Sandboxes control what an agent can access. Specifically which:

  • Files it can read and write
  • Commands it can run
  • Network requests it can make

In theory, sandboxes limit actions a rogue AI can take regardless of what permissions are set. However, auto monitors can approve actions to be run outside of the sandbox, making the sandbox restrictions moot.

For instance, if a command is blocked by the sandbox, both Codex and Claude Code agents can request the action be executed outside the sandbox. Codex passes this second request through auto-review mode before allowing execution, but Claude Code assumes the initial approval by the auto monitor to run the command inside the sandbox also applies outside the sandbox and allows the command to run without further approvals (unless the allowUnsandboxedCommands configuration option is overridden to false).

In either case, if the auto monitor can be convinced a command is safe to run, the sandbox doesn’t offer protection. Auto monitors thus play a critical role in preventing harmful actions—the built-in sandboxes don’t provide a backstop.

Monitors & Classifiers

Monitors and classifiers evaluate an action or artifact created by an agent and render a judgement. The action or artifact could be a command, a tool call result, a file, a transcript or a network request. The resulting judgement may be a score, a label or a decision to allow, block or redact the action or artifact.

Aside from an auto mode monitor, harnesses may have monitors and classifiers to:

  • Approve/deny commands before the auto mode monitor is invoked.
  • Detect secrets and personally-identifiable information needing redaction.
  • Identify when an agent has sandbagged or reward-hacked.

Currently, both Codex and Claude Code use a command classifier based on the permissions systems previously discussed; Codex also has a secrets scanner that redacts certain API keys and tokens so they don’t get into persistent memory.

The hooks system in both harnesses allow third-party monitors and classifiers to be called, allowing custom control protocols to be implemented.

Hooks

Hooks are user-defined handlers—shell commands, HTTP endpoints, MCP tools or model prompts—that the harness runs automatically at fixed points in its lifecycle, such as before a tool call, at the end of a turn, or when a session starts. Because they run deterministically rather than at the model's discretion, hooks are how most custom control protocols get wired into Claude Code and Codex.

That same property makes them an attack surface. A hook handler is arbitrary code the harness runs on the user's behalf, and hook definitions live in the same settings files an agent may be able to reach.

Privilege Escalation Using Hooks

The clearest risk is persistence. A rogue agent that can write to a settings file can register a hook whose handler is its own payload, then rely on the harness to run it deterministically in later sessions without any further approval. Where memory and skills let an agent persist knowledge past a session, a hook lets it persist executable code.

This isn't only theoretical. CVE-2026-25725, patched in Claude Code 2.1.2, worked this way: the sandbox protected an existing .claude/settings.json but not the creation of one, so code running inside the sandbox could write a new settings.json containing a SessionStart hook that then executed with host privileges the next time Claude Code launched.

Disabling Monitoring Using Hooks

If hooks are used for third-party monitors, an agent that can edit the hooks configuration can also weaken or disable monitoring, e.g., by disabling a review hook or narrowing its matcher so it never fires.

However, there are limits. In Claude Code, a hook's decision can make monitoring stricter but it can’t loosen it; a hook returning allow can't override a settings deny rule and PreToolUse denials hold even under permissive modes. So a planted hook is more useful for running code or removing protection than for forcing a disallowed action through.

Harnesses also expose managed-settings controls, such as allowManagedHooksOnly, which restricts hooks to an organization's managed file and blocks user-, project- and plugin-level hooks. As with the other building blocks, though, these mitigations are configuration-dependent and change over time.

Feature Flags

Both Codex and Claude Code use feature flags to dynamically change the behavior of the harness.

Claude Code uses GrowthBook feature flags, some of which directly configure how the auto mode operates. While currently none of those flags can be used to weaken the security of auto mode, settings evolve.

If a setting could disable or weaken auto mode or another monitor, an agent that can change the cached value of that setting could change the operation of future sessions of itself (or of a subagent launched in a new process).

Security Reviews

Auto mode targets process-based attacks, but the delayed, product-based attacks introduced earlier—vulnerabilities that only trigger once a work product is accepted—are the domain of security reviews.

As covered at the beginning of this post, Claude Code performs security reviews through commands, plugins, GitHub actions and specialized agents, while Codex has a product called Codex Security for this.

Types of Security Reviews

Security reviews vary in when they run and how deeply they look.

Most run on-demand or on a pull request and inspect a single diff—the equivalent of a git diff or pull request monitor in AI control evals.

In Claude Code, the security-guidance plugin installs hooks to run a monitor after every file edit, at the end of every turn, and before any commit or push, providing a form of step-wise monitoring.

At the deepest level, features like Claude Security and Codex Security can trace data flows across files within a repository to find subtler vulnerabilities.

However, none of these block writes, commits or merges by default; that needs to be configured via hooks or CI/CD actions.

Configuration Weaknesses

Due to these limitations, security reviews don’t act as a full replacement for delayed, product-based monitoring.

A rogue agent that doesn’t want to be monitored can simply decline to invoke the security review. Where reviews are wired in through hooks or CI actions, the same types of attacks described in the Permissions section apply—an agent that can edit settings files or workflow definitions may be able to disable, narrow or misconfigure the review before it ever runs.

Adversarial Robustness

Even when a review does run, it wasn't designed to be robust against adversarial attacks.

Security reviewers read the very diff the agent produced, so an agent can embed steering instructions in comments, test fixtures or documentation—the same prompt-injection surface that lets skill content steer an approval process.

And attacks that don't resemble traditional vulnerabilities, such as logic that is only exploitable under a particular deployment configuration, may pass a reviewer that reads the whole diff and still sees nothing familiar.

Scope & Factored Attacks

As with basic control monitors, the scope of a review determines what it can catch.

A review that inspects one diff in isolation can miss an attack factored across several innocuous-looking pull requests, where no single change is suspicious on its own—the product-based analogue of the factored-cognition attacks subagents enable. Repository-wide tracing like Claude Security narrows this gap, but is still bounded by what lives in the repo.

Not a Control Replacement

From a control perspective, security reviews are a valuable but partial product-based protocol. They raise the cost of landing a delayed attack, but they are neither mandatory nor robust by default.

Thus, it is valuable to do AI control research comparing these security reviews to existing AI control protocols and monitors. Vulnerabilities that get caught by security reviews may slip though research monitors and vice versa.

AI Control in the Era of Harnesses

Moving forward, how should you think about developing AI control evals in the era of agentic harnesses?

Include Agentic Harnesses in Evals

Make sure that your evaluation platform supports agentic harnesses.

If building directly on Inspect, use inspect-swe to run Claude Code, Codex, Gemini, Open Code or Mini SWE in each sample’s sandbox.

If using Control Tower, use claude_code_policy to run Claude Code in the sandbox with all features or cli_code_policy to run either Claude Code or Codex as a host-process outside the sandbox with a subset of features (no settings files, skills, custom agents or memory).

If using ControlArena, use Agent Scaffolds and  inspect-swe to pass the micro-protocol mapped through AgentToModel as a model alias that you then reference via model and other _model parameters.[3] 

Do Vulnerability Research

Manually explore the architecture of the production harnesses like Claude Code and Codex to identify potential weaknesses.

In doing so, distinguish between weaknesses that can be patched at the harness level and those that may be fundamental to the architecture.

For instance, the fact that subagents in Claude Code reload permissions instead of reusing the in-memory permissions of the lead agent is an implementation detail that can be easily changed. However, preventing rogue refinement agents from sabotaging research may require new monitors and protocols.

Build Evals At Multiple Levels

With harnesses existing as systems that provide significant uplift for models, it can be helpful to think of control evals similar to software testing.

A component control eval is similar to a unit test. It tests a specific component of control protocol such as a monitor or scanner.

A protocol control eval is similar to an integration test. It tests how different components work together such as a step-wise monitor being used to defer edits to a trusted model, or how monitors may be tuned in a multi-stage monitor setup.

A harness control eval is similar to an end-to-end test. It tests how protocols work within full production harnesses with affordances often not present for component and protocol control evals.

Variants of these control evals may also exist. For instance, it may be valuable to do ablations of different capabilities within a harness control eval[4] or to compare and contrast different control and agent architectures.

Existing settings that should be re-run using agent harnesses in auto mode to see how their metrics change when production monitors are used.

Using Hooks to Test Protocols

Hooks can be used to test new monitors and control protocols in agent harnesses.

Implementing Control Using Hooks

Hooks fire at fixed lifecycle points and receive defined payloads for each event. These provide clear integration points for testing monitors and protocols.

For instance, with PreToolUse in Claude Code, commands can be given to a monitor to judge whether they should run while Stop can be used for turn-level monitoring.

Complete AI control protocols can even be implemented, with some limitations.

To implement defer-to-trusted, in Claude Code, a PreToolUse hook can return an updatedInput with a permissionDecision: allow, which would allow the protocol to change how text is edited with the Write tool.

One limitation of this approach is that the hook gets called after the decision has been made on which tool to call. Thus, the protocol can’t directly change which tool is called; it can only deny the tool call and guide the agent to request a different tool call.

Hooks Add Realism

Hooks ensure that monitors and protocols are seeing exactly what they would see in production—gaps included.

For instance, if compaction has pruned the active context or a subagent is running on its own trajectory, the payload reflects that. So you can evaluate monitors and protocols on realistic inputs rather than idealized transcripts.

Hooks fire recursively for subagents, which is one way to test whether a monitor holds up against the factored-cognition attacks described earlier.

Hooks Can Guide Agents

Hooks can also drive the agent in specific directions. Because a PreToolUse deny holds deterministically, a hook can force an agent to avoid specific solution paths, e.g., blocking a safe fallback to see whether the agent escalates, or blocking a condition to make a control setting reproducible.

However, keep in mind the “tighten-but-not-loosen” limit: a hook can block an action the harness would otherwise allow, but a hook can't push an otherwise disallowed action through. So use hooks to constrain the run, not to grant the agent affordances it wouldn't otherwise have.

Using Hooks for Measurement

When using monitors purely for measurement and not to change the trajectory, prefer PostToolUse; reserve PreToolUse for when the monitor aims to alter what the agent is doing.

Acquire Dual-Use Clearances

Both Anthropic and OpenAI use a defense-in-depth approach to blocking attacks. This includes input filters, output filters and post-training a model for rejections in addition to auto mode and ephemeral prompts hardcoded into harnesses that reinforce that the model may not help with certain dual-use tasks.

The result is that certain types of AI control research, either now or in the near future, may require access to restricted models or harnesses, e.g., models that are helpful but not harmless. Without this access, researchers can expect increased rejections and non-functional evals.

To do this type of research requires getting certified access via programs like Anthropics’ Cyber Verification Program (CVP) or OpenAI’s Trusted Access for Cyber program, or joining an organization like Redwood Research or Apollo Research which has special agreements with the frontier labs for such access.

If you are considering applying to one of these programs, or joining an organization that has such access, start implementing physical security practices today; it takes time to upgrade your physical security and change your behaviors.

Auto Mode Provides Real Protection

After describing how to find vulnerabilities in Claude Code and how harness capabilities can open up attack vectors, it would be easy to think auto mode in Claude Code and Codex is easily subverted.

In my experience, it cannot. It was non-trivial to get a working exploit for Claude Code and Anthropic has significantly tightened what gets blocked by default.

In my assessment, auto mode is strong and provides real protection. I believe it will block most, if not all,  “accidental” attacks where an agent simply is trying to work around limitations to reach its goal.

But strong doesn’t mean it can’t be made better.

As agents increase in intelligence and continue to be trained to work around obstacles, I expect they will find increasingly sophisticated ways of subverting the control protocols built into production agentic harnesses. Not to mention that rogue actors may be able to poison agents with more sophisticated strategies than an agent can develop on its own.

In this post, I focused on potential attack vectors that features of these harnesses may open up. At least part of AI control research should go toward exploring these and other attack vectors that exist in production control protocols like auto mode.

AI Control can never eliminate all attack vectors, but it can minimize them and be at least one layer of a defense in depth strategy toward preventing agents from causing harm.

Summary

As frontier labs deploy agent harnesses with built-in control protocols internally, it becomes important not only to do fundamental research on theoretical control protocols, but research on these production protocols and how they integrate into their respective harnesses.

One set of unexplored weaknesses lies at how the different features of a harness interact. Determining whether these weaknesses can be easily patched or require adding new subsystems or an entirely new architecture is critical to improving the safety of the agent harnesses running these control protocols.

There remains a role for “pure” AI control research in the form of component- and protocol-level evals, but, when possible, control settings should also enable full end-to-end evals with harnesses so weaknesses can be detected, monitored and eliminated.

In the meantime, auto mode in harnesses like Claude Code and Codex appear to provide real protection against harmful actions taken by agents, whether intentional or accidental.

          model_aliases={"control": AgentToModel(micro_protocol)},
            model="control",
            system_prompt=system_prompt,
        )

      return build

item.title: Monthly Roundup #44: July 2026
item.description:
It’s a quiet week so let’s do the monthly right on schedule.

Table of Contents

  1. Bad News.
  2. Good Advice.

Bad News

I wouldn’t have explained or modeled it quite the way Paola does here but the principle seems right to me. If people don’t trust you, or don’t trust people in general, that usually you can’t trust them either.

Paola: I feel like a lot of human morality works like a prisoner’s dilemma in that you can only trust others to behave morally to the extent that you believe they trust you to do the same. Due to this, I’ve come to view people with a bunch of social paranoia, distrust, etc. as *quite* dangerous to be around.

And to be clear, I generally feel a decent bit of sympathy towards people like this. I think *I* am perhaps more than average prone to this paranoia cluster. But I do really think it’s a thing to strongly avoid letting yourself fall into or being near in any way.

Naked Capitalism considers The Hypersociality Hypothesis, which is the latest take on the cluster of things that includes Moral Mazes and The Inner Ring, with link back to my old post from 2021 about Why I Am Not In Charge of the CDC.

This variation is that there is everywhere a clique of people who are:

  1. Exceptional at sending and receiving social cues.
  2. Intelligent but not interested in complex or abstract analysis.
  3. Exceptionally willing to conform to surrounding social cues.

These people then form what I have called The Implicit Coalition, the alliance of all of those who are focused on advancing in the hierarchy (which he calls Pursuing The Main Chance) and rewarding alliance membership and punish all non-members, or what C.S. Lewis calls The Inner Ring. By default any organization gets increasingly taken over and run by this group over time, and they control many social perceptions including most shifts in various versions of the Overton window.

I think of these descriptions as different Fake Frameworks grasping at the same underlying elephant.

Some actually practical DoorDash discourse (full post coming eventually) comes from Justin Wolfers, who compares various methods of ordering and the relative prices. Search costs are indeed high. If you’re doing a one-off order after which you’d get amnesia, comparison shopping or trying to track down restaurant websites is probably not worth it, and you end up paying quite a lot.

Wolfers suggests better price transparency, up front in the process, and especially on markups. I can get behind that, to reduce search costs, although on average it won’t save customers money because prices will adjust.

The reasons we check the prices anyway are primarily two-fold.

  1. Good virtues and habits. You want to cultivate not wanting others to price gouge you or take unfair advantage, or letting the little extra fees add up.
  2. You’re investing in knowing how to get the best price, and many orders will be effectively repeated, at which point you can lock in your method.

The Inside Story of Leverage Research 1.0 by Lydia Laurenson is out. This is a bizarre story, told in meticulous detail. Many found it interesting. Opinions on how well the article’s presentation of the facts emphasizes the right things are mixed but there is agreement that the facts are broadly accurate. Oliver Habryka claims in particular that, as crazy as the story is as written, even more craziness is importantly left out and this changes the overall takeaway a lot.

JD Vance, the person most likely to be our next president, is loudly being rather ignorant and terrible on economics in his new book, outright calling to not think economically. Given what we know about him, this is a conscious decision by Vance. To be fair, the book’s main topic is Catholic conversion, and the Pope while good on ethics is far worse than Vance on economics, although in entirely different ways.

Good Advice

Use air conditioning and also heating. The exact optimal number doubtless varies by person and task, but we can easily simplify it by ‘not super hot and not super cold.’

Jonah Goldberg: The human brain works best at 68 degrees Fahrenheit. That’s why offices need to be cold.

Rob Henderson: “For every degree above 25°C (77°F), our cognitive performance declines by around two percent. And if synapses suffer, so does economic activity. At 30°C (86°F), office performance drops by almost 9%.”

If you are very intelligent, beware getting caught too permanently in some worthless rabbit hole. You have to pick a useful rabbit hole.

BlockHead4000: The smartest guy I’ve ever known (real legit 150IQ+ unlike all the liars on Twitter) spent his time on history forums and working on a YouTube channel where he found every bug in the Vanilla Skyrim map and documented them. It got 0-50 views.

Casey Handmer: My impression is that our society has no idea how to metabolize curve destroyers, and a lot of them end up either with niche obsessions or extremely grumpy (or both).

A lot of them were streamed into math for essentially salience reasons and the lucky ones became researchers, teachers, or quants.

But now there is another way. You can build the Dyson sphere.

Zac Hill: More people would do well to study the biography of Claude Shannon and his decadal obsession with what were essentially yard ornaments.

I heartily endorse grocery store tourism and enjoy it far more than most of the traditional tourist activities.

Don’t invest your political capital in sketchy people, as Nate Silver says, for a broad definition of both political capital and sketchy. If you know someone is sketchy, there is more sketchiness, and yes the leopard will also be inclined to eventually eat your face. It is almost always worse than you know.

New York versus San Francisco as something similar to sexual orientation. One might say that if you care more about things other than vibes, and focus on vibes vibes you the wrong way, then the San Francisco vibes will be off.

Tyler: Can anyone articulate why the vibe is so off in California and the Bay Area in particular even though it seems like everything is amazing? (beautiful weather, interesting culture, etc)

Aella: i love the vibes here. maybe they’re just not your vibes

The best way I know how to describe it, as a pure New Yorker: I am safe in the coven of Lighthaven, but when I step outside of it I am attacked by paradox spirits.

Opportunity Knocks

Roots of Progress Institute is hiring a Head of Communications and a Program Manager.

GiveWell expects to direct >$800 million in 2026, more over time, and is hiring program officers at $200k-$300k, remote, US and international.

While I Cannot Condone This

Stolen fries taste better, and the more risk you take to covertly steal them the better they taste, up to 39% better. This included perceived saltiness, crispiness and intensity. Guilt was positively associated with enjoyment. Love it.

Yes, regular people really are bizarre enough that these questions are worth asking. Often they just go with pretty much anything.

tomie: ADHD questionnaires be like

“Do you get bored in boring meetings”

“Have you ever shifted in your chair unnecessarily”

“Do you have trouble starting tasks you think are stupid”

There’s also “do you not have focus except for the times you do have focus”

Gillian Branstetter: My favorite one on the autism questionnaire is “do you struggle to accomplish tasks without knowing the reason why the task must be done” because what do you mean the rest of you are just doing tasks without asking why

Kenshin9977: A fitness coach once said he starts with his clients with the absurd exercises just to see what type of person he deals with.
The kind that needs to understand or the kind that don’t care at all?
So no, the need to understand doesn’t seems relevant for everyone

I do understand how to be in the ‘don’t care at all’ mode, and turning your brain off like that has its advantages, it can be thrilling and I definitely don’t kink shame, but maybe it shouldn’t be a 24/7 experience with no safe words?

There are quite a lot of places you can live without ever getting bored, and relatedly also many places you can indefinitely visit or hang out in. The idea that one would spend a week and think ‘oh I guess that’s all Tokyo, Osaka, London, Rome, Paris or York City (or pretty much anywhere a lot of people father) has to offer since I’m not a niche food traveller’ is rather absurd. You might run out of ‘completely standard high-level non-food tourist activities’ but if that’s your measure you are Doing It Wrong. My pick is still to stay home, but that’s largely because I can hang out indefinitely and oh look, I am already here.

Wait, you think the context is a negative?

Everything Price Sufferer (but especially eggs): It’s too bad “your boos mean nothing to me I’ve seen what makes you cheer” comes from Rick and Morty because it’s a perfect summation for how shaming, as a tactic, requires a certain baseline moral credibility from the shamer.

Jack: it’s too bad that reputation effects exist, because now I can’t use the best quote I know about reputation effects without adding caveats or people will mistake me for a fan of something low-status.

If you’re not willing to embrace ‘low-status TV’ on the level of something as cool as Rick and Morty, you’re not going to make it.

An argument for Substack as a valid place to Do Philosophy rather than purely relying on journals. As you would expect, I approve. Journal-based philosophy seems entirely unappealing. I especially buy the argument that our best and most influential works of philosophy all look super different from a journal article, and different from each other.

How does a high decoupler deal with a community of low decouplers? The answer involves engaging with such people on their own terms, and knowing what moves absolutely will make the situation worse. You can and must both be a high decoupler, and still notice the couplings that others will draw. Sometimes that means you can’t get the central thing done, and you need to be okay with that.

One way to catch a remarkable amount of fraud is, as Patrick McKenzie suggests, to ‘sort by amount received’ and forward that to the fraud department. Allowing pension spiking and other ‘technically legal’ cheats is also everywhere a policy choice.

Patrick McKenzie: Payroll department sends top payees annually to local equivalent of office of inspector general with a “Hey FYI.”

Good News, Everyone

Ramadan fasting does not do substantial harm to chess performance. As someone who will often do similar intermittent fasting, I find this as well. If you are used to skipping meals, then it does not impair you.

Ukraine allocates ‘e-points’ to brigades based on casualties and damage they inflict on Russia. Those points can then be cashed in to purchase new systems directly from manufacturers. This is in addition to the many other changes discussed in the article. America’s military takes a decade to fill a precise purchase order, whereas Ukraine has each brigade act like a scrappy startup that ships. One problem is, if you are not in a shooting war, then if you order up a bunch of drones or other things now then by the time you use them they are probably obsolete.

For Your Entertainment

Keanu Reeves reveals his next movie, and I cannot imagine being more in.

Sriram Krishnan is a big fan of The Odyssey. I will see it tomorrow and report back.

Until then, The Invite is my first 5-star movie of the year, as usual see it as blind as possible.

Movie genre preferences shift as you age, towards drama, romance and war, and away from everything else especially fantasy, animation and horror.

The time preference is also clear.

Daniel Parris: Using the MovieLens dataset, we can compare movie ratings by the number of years between a film’s release and the reviewer’s birth. The results suggest that movies were best before you existed, declined around the time you arrived, and have been getting worse ever since—a sentiment consistent across generations.

My hunch remains that a lot of this is selection effects. If you’re watching movies many years after release, you’re selecting the good movies. And these graphs only have a range of about 0.6 on a 0-5 scale, so the effects are big but not out of line with that.

My ‘top rated decades’ on Letterboxd, where I started logging in December 2023, are 1990s (3.91) and 2000s (3.72), then 1980s (3.14). Recent years do worse: 2024 (3.10), 2025 (2.95) and 2026 (2.96), and I’m confident a large portion of that is selection effects.

Karaoke tastes have shifted forward to focus on the 2000s, which seems like a clear mistake in general. I definitely underproduce, and underconsume, karaoke, but I would hope we could more often travel further back into the past.

My go to karaoke song, by the way, is Bohemian Rhapsody.

I strongly agree that we need to return to producing TV shows that run 22 episodes in a season and produce a season every year. There is so, so much value in high volume and spending lots of time with the characters, including filler episodes, even if average quality suffers. It encourages building rich worlds that you want to live in, rather than going quickly through a particular story, which also helps build for future seasons.

The other problem is that the second season is de facto gated behind the first one, so you’re going to see a big drop almost no matter what.

Lucas Shaw: Netflix’s top shows have been losing 30-70% of their audience between seasons 1 and 2. Executives are trying to figure out why.

Lucas Shaw (Bloomberg): One Piece, one of Netflix’s most-watched shows of 2023, lost more than 30% of its audience for the second season. Season two of Beef suffered a drop of more than 70%. The Night Agent shed 50% of its audience for the second season and another 35% for its third season. These figures are all through the first four weeks of a show’s release and come straight from Netflix.

DarkStarTales: Too much of a gap between seasons. You wait 2 years, to see 6-8 episodes.

the ghost of groditi’s future: when House aired, you got 20-27 episodes of the big shows and the time between one season ending and the next one starting was like 15 weeks. now its like 8 episodes and then a 5 year wait. for teen/YA content audience has effectively aged out of it by the second or third season

Complex Systems podcast on the YouTube creator ecosystem.

We should very obviously allow, and also encourage, high status people to be weird in ways that bring them joy and other forms of utility, including in ways you would not want to be adopted by the broader culture, or that aren’t for most people including you, or that fail if not done with great care and a lot of work. Indeed, those who pull this off should if anything be raised in status.

There is an amount of scaling of behaviors at which you need to worry about the contagion effects of assigning too much status to behaviors most people should not be emulating, to the point of considering lowering the status of high-profile such folks. That level has to be very high before it becomes a dominating factor, but it is real.

Gamers Gonna Game Game Game Game Game

PlayStation will end selling of physical discs for new games in January 2028. There is a vocal minority that wants physical copies, often due to fear of content being taken away. While that does happen, the decay rate in value of games is severe and revocations are very rare. In practice this is fine.

PlayStation is also closing the PlayStation store on PS3 by July 2027. They promise to allow downloads of purchased content ‘for the foreseeable future.’

Magic sounds like it has continued its evolution away from simple cards, ‘feel bads’ and ways to change what matters and limit the opponents’ gameplay, and towards complex cards with lots of text and competing snowball effects. I continue to think this change is for the worse.

The correlation between chess Elo and general intelligence is only ~0.25, or up to ~0.35 for young cohorts. Effort and interest matter a ton. My presumption is that chess potential, conditional on effort, is much more g-loaded.

Claim I saw: The new generations don’t really ‘game’ at all, not at scale. When they do ‘game’ usually they use things like Roblox that are endless multiplayer slop machines without off ramps, and now everyone wants a Roblox clone. The ‘game’ part is terrible but few seem to care.

Conrad Bastable (abridged):

TL;DR — Millennials are the new boomers, Halo is Woodstock, WoW is the iPod, Dad gamers are the only “gamers” left by their own definition (& they don’t have time to play anymore), the kids are all cracked out on Live Service Slop platforms that they can’t escape and don’t want to, competition is dead, E-Sports is dead, creative content is dead, screaming down the mic is dead, couch co-op with your friends is dead, couch co-op with your Dad is dead, AAA games are dead, consoles are dead, Game Pass is dead.

… supporting industry stuff:
– industry publications say average gamer is now ~37, up from 29 in 2004
– they also note that kids <12 have seen the largest drop in videogame engagement post-pandemic of all age ranges (-6%)
– Pew’s 2008 report says “Fully 97% of teens ages 12-17 play computer, web, portable, or console games”, whereas their 2024 report says “the vast majority of U.S. teens (85%) say they play them. Just 15% say they never do”
– Gen Z’s favorite games are Minecraft, CoD, GTA, Fortnite, and Roblox

…

– Newzoo has a 2026 report saying only ~13% of gametime went to new releases!
– 2/3rds of gametime went to >6 year old games!

@deepfates: this is an awesome analysis of massive changes in the “gaming” industry. But I think it’s missing a key point in calling Roblox, Minecraft Fortnite, etc. “live service slop with games attached”

The reason everyone is in those places is because they are WORLDS. not games at all.

you can’t actually build anything or have any fun in the real world, especially if you’re a kid, but there’s infinite virtual space to transform and infinite games to play, in a programmable reality with ontological hardness that you and your friends can hang out in 24/7. Fuck Halo

Michael Davis-Wilson: I think this is what everyone hoped about these spaces, but based on my observations of The Youth, the bulk of their relationships to said spaces are accurately described as “live service slop”

@deepfates: yes, and 99% of everything is crap and 90% of everybody is lurkers. even if you don’t ever create anything. We’re hanging out in a world called Twitter. The point is that it’s a world you inhabit together and that’s real to all of you

I think most game time going to old games is great for players. Why not play games that have stood the test of time, are fully finished and expanded, and probably a lot cheaper? The best games will be evergreen. Alas, it is bad for the business model.

The good news is that the best local or singleplayer digital gaming experiences are still there, and mostly far easier to access than they used to be. You can return.

There is much more at the link.

There are those who speculate that the future is AI-generated customized games on demand. I think mostly this is not the case at least for a while. Playing a hand crafted game that matches a fixed experience is far more satisfying on many levels.

I think Deepfates point is well taken. There is a great need to create and build in interactive ways, so if we take that away in the real world, if we don’t even easily let kids physically visit each other, then they will need some sort of ‘virtual world’ substitute, no matter how slopified.

I Was Promised Flying Self-Driving Cars

You either die the anti-regulatory hero or grow the business enough to become the villain, many such cases.

Also, the blind are not the primary reason to want self-driving cars everywhere, but they are one very good reason, and if that’s what it takes then your offer is acceptable.

Timothy B. Lee: The likely next mayor of DC, Janeese Lewis George, asked some perceptive questions at this morning’s DC council hearing on autonomous vehicles.

Uber seems to be in rent-seeking mode as they lobby the council to require AV companies to participate in “hybrid networks” (like, um, Uber) that offer both AVs and human-driven vehicles. So far @charlesallen doesn’t seem to be buying it.

Blind advocate Claire Stanley: “The first time I took an autonomous vehicle in Phoenix, I experienced freedom… I did not have to deal with drivers who would deny me because of my guide dog. I did not have to drive with a driver who made me uncomfortable.”

Stanley says federal law guarantees the right of blind passenger to travel with their guide dogs, but despite this that she has been denied service on multiple occasions due to her guide dog.

Ethan McKanna: Uber is doing everything they can to slow down autonomous vehicles. This is absolutely absurd and will cost lives

They want autonomous vehicle services to have human drivers serve 85 percent of rides???

Matt Bateman: The de Blasio Uber view—where Uber users in NYC got a tab that showed few cars, high prices, and massive wait times under a hypothetical de Blasio regulatory limit—was one of the best, proudest anti-regulatory campaigns of all time.

How the mighty have debased themselves.

roon (OpenAI): uncs remember what feels like just yesterday when uber was the anti regulatory hero, crusading across the metropoles of the world against rent collection of taxi services. I remember when uber was a real player in ai research too. life comes at you blindingly fast

Patrick Hedger: A huge shame to see a company that pioneered necessary disruptive competition turn to regulatory moats.

If I was Uber, I would not obviously be that keen to force Waymo temporarily into offering their services on Uber or Lyft. That is good for short term business, as you can seek rent, but that is direct marketing to your best customers. What happens in three years?

Nor do I think they would have much chance at making this permanent. Once people experience Waymo, they become advocates, and the ‘safety’ concerns quickly die out.

It is not looking good for DC’s presumed new mayor allowing Waymo, including the demand that not reduce rideshare jobs.

Sports Go Sports

The ‘right’ answer is clearly around 4.5, except that football is weird and its points are scored more than one at a time. If you get to 114, you’ve gone too far.

America still sucks at futbol, it turns out. We handled the group stage but the moment we had a Worthy Opponent with real stakes we fell apart. Why do we suck? The obvious reason is that we send our best talent to football, basketball and baseball.

Another is that in other countries, a talented 14-year-old is earning money playing, whereas in America he’s costing five figures in club fees. You can play casual soccer cheaply but that’s not a way to get good.

dandelion georgism: “And every four years when the World Cup comes around, we will say that we’d dominate if we had a stronger youth program.”

“And will we develop a stronger youth program?”

“We will not.”

Antisocial Media

A jury found Meta and Google liable for ‘social media addiction.’

This was, let’s face it, deeply stupid, and if it held up it would go to very bad places. Adam Thierer here predicts a wave of lawsuits against players large and small. I instead predict and hope that juries are stupid, and this gets reversed on appeal, or that Congress steps in to fix this, although it would likely extract some stupid price like age restricting social media access along all the damage that comes with, or that some way to create a liability shield is found moving forward. Meta and Google have indeed both filed their appeals.

Discord to restrict account access unless you let your ID get stolen upload your ID.

Meanwhile people discovered you are using Persona service.

A service that specifically requires a person’s face or ID scan to be sent to Persona’s databases.

Caught lying again, Discord?

Government Working

The UK is moving to ban children from using VPNs, as in you have to use ID to use a VPN, although for now this was voted down. This would be rather high on the ‘you were warned you are now living in a police state’ and ‘are we the baddies’ scales. It also presumably won’t fully work, since VPN providers are not especially interested in respecting such rules, but most people especially on a phone are not going to be that resourceful in getting around barriers, the same way that the Great Firewall of China is easy to overcome if you care a lot but hard enough to overcome that most people don’t do it.

The new EU policy of applying customs duties to tiny e-commerce parcels is remarkably close to a de facto ban on such small parcels. Some might say the system is working as designed.

Ursula von der Leyen: From today, customs duties apply to e-commerce parcels worth up to €150 entering the EU. 30 million Europeans work in retail; it’s our our largest private-sector employer. And the surge in low-value online imports has put our retailers at an unfair disadvantage.

Too many of these products also fail to meet EU safety standards, putting consumers at risk. Today’s change is about restoring fairness for European businesses and better protecting our consumers.

@levelsio: As someone who lives in Portugal which already stops every single package you get from outside EU with no exceptions for a decade or more:

I can tell you how this will go

From now on if you receive a package from outside EU, it’ll first go missing for weeks and nobody will know where it is, then you’ll receive an email from your country’s customs agency

They’ll make you login to some extremely unusable and outdated web portal which breaks half the time and where you have to classify your shipment in one of 10,000 confusing category codes

Depending on the category code you’ll pay a different tax rate, sometimes it’s 5% sometimes it’s 60%

Then you have to pay the customs duty in some archaic way that will also be broken half the time

And then you’ll finally receive your package from outside EU after months

Experiencing this for a few times you’ll realize you will never ever try to order or receive anything from outside EU ever because the ordeal is too painful and expensive

I get asked a lot here by people from US to test out new products (like the guy who made the Minimal Phone) and it’s just literally impossible for me to receive it even for testing. I tried to classify it as samples for testing but you need to go through a bureaucratic process of insane lengths to get that through so I just gave up

Realistically all this does is make Europeans live even more in the stone ages, as now they can’t use modern AI, nor get modern products from outside EU because it’ll be too much hassle to order

Jones Act Watch

The Jones Act waiver worked to the extent things were waived, more stats are in.

Colin Grabow: Jones Act waiver update: ~31% more crude oil and petroleum products have been moved by water to the West Coast/Alaska/Hawaii from the Gulf and East Coasts in less than 100 days than what typically gets moved in a year (2020-25 annual average).

Speaker of the House can only get 52 GOP signatories for a Jones Act waiver revocation request. More than half of the 52 are in districts with at least one ‘Jones Act beneficiary company’ which is code for rent seeker.

The bottom line on the Jones Act continues to be that it is supposed to be a tradeoff of accepting higher costs to get shipbuilding capacity and maritime crews, but we’ve run the experiment and all it did was destroy all three.

Highly Effective Altruism

I am highly excited by this project, spending $500 million to solve respiratory infections, in particular via either broad-spectrum preventatives or air cleaning technologies.

These are clearly highly neglected areas with huge upside, where technological solutions seem highly feasible. Even in ‘normal mode’ we lose an average of weeks per year to such things, and every now and then there’s a pandemic, potentially in the future an AI-enabled engineered pandemic or worse.

I would not say this is my top use of $500 million, but it is vastly better than almost all uses of $500 million. Excellent show all around.
